questions.topic: A source that cannot be obtained
questions.learningObjective: Handle a citation to a source that has been withdrawn

stimulus.body: Footnote 3 cites a modelling report that the publisher has withdrawn after an error was found in its second table. The planner's paragraph uses the figure from that table to argue that the corridor needs four lanes.

questions.stem: What should the planner do with the paragraph that relies on the withdrawn figure?

options.text: Keep the paragraph but flag that the source was withdrawn, since readers should know the history.
options.misconception: keeps a known bad figure on transparency grounds

options.text: Remove the figure and rebuild the argument on the data the planner can verify, and say what was dropped.
Substitute a similar figure from an older report on the same corridor and keep the argument intact.
options.misconception: swaps in a number that has no bearing on the claim

options.text: Keep the figure but add the author's note that the table has since been corrected.
options.misconception: asserts a correction the planner has not seen

questions.explanation: A figure known to be wrong cannot support an argument, and flagging it does not repair the reasoning built on it. Rebuilding on verifiable data is the honest route.
questions.hint: A known bad figure cannot carry an argument.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A citation offered for a work nobody in the room has read
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a genuinely unread source from a doubtful one
questions.stem: A planner cites a 2020 working paper that nobody has read but which a colleague says is well regarded in the field. Which judgement is most defensible?

options.text: The citation may well point to a good source, but it cannot support a claim until someone reads it.
A colleague's report of the paper's standing is enough for the citation to be used.
options.misconception: substitutes second-hand reputation for the writer's reading

options.text: The citation should be dropped because unread sources are never citable in academic work.
options.misconception: states a ban where the problem is a condition of reading

options.text: The citation is sound because working papers are drafts and cannot be wrong in a way that matters.
options.misconception: assumes drafts carry no risk of error

questions.explanation: A citation may be well chosen and still be unusable by a writer who has not read it. Reputation reported by a colleague and the assumption that drafts are safe replace the reading needed.
questions.hint: Good reputation is not a substitute for the reading itself.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A reading response that paraphrases and never judges
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a disguised judgement inside a supposedly neutral response
questions.stem: A response says only that the author describes a parking levy accurately and that the levy described would be difficult to implement. Which reading of that response is most accurate?

options.text: The response is a neutral summary, since it reports the book without adding the writer's view.
options.misconception: takes a stated difficulty as nothing more than reportage

options.text: The response contains a judgement, because calling the levy difficult to implement assesses it.
The response is a summary of the author's opinion rather than of the author's evidence.
options.misconception: misses that the difficulty judgement is the writer's own

options.text: The response would become a judgement if it also described the book's central argument.
options.misconception: assumes judgement needs an account of the argument

questions.explanation: Judgement appears wherever the writer evaluates rather than merely reports, and calling a policy difficult to implement is such an evaluation. It is small, but it can be disputed.
questions.hint: Look for any assessment the writer has made, however brief.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a citation has to let a reader do
questions.learningObjective: State the minimum a citation must enable a reader to do
questions.stem: A planner argues that the minimum requirement of any citation in a planning paper is that the reader be able to find and read the source for the claim. Which claim best supports that requirement?

options.text: Citations mainly protect the planner from blame if the claim turns out to be wrong.
options.misconception: treats citations as insurance rather than as evidence

options.text: Citations mainly let readers judge the quality of the planner's reading on the subject.
options.misconception: makes the citation a test of the writer, not the claim

options.text: A citation is useful only when it lets a reader check the claim it is attached to.
Citations matter mainly because reference lists are required by the office's style guide.
options.misconception: grounds the practice in house style rather than in reading

questions.explanation: The point of attaching a source to a claim is to let a reader test the claim rather than take it on trust. Blame avoidance, reputation and style rules are not the evidential reason.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader can do about the claim after reading it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A position held and then given up
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a withdrawn position is part of a writer's usable record
questions.stem: A planner has withdrawn a recommendation on night bus service. In two or three sentences, explain why the withdrawn recommendation belongs in the planner's published record.

answer.exemplar: The withdrawn recommendation shows what the planner argued, on what grounds, and where that argument no longer holds, which lets readers who met it know exactly what to stop relying on. It also lets the planner show how the position changed, which is what makes the current position credible rather than arbitrary.

questions.explanation: A record that excludes withdrawn claims makes the office's thinking unreadable and leaves earlier readers with outdated guidance. Showing the change makes the present position intelligible.
questions.hint: Readers who met the old claim need to see it withdrawn.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a record should show about a changed position
questions.learningObjective: Check a briefing note for what it records about a changed position

stimulus.body: Briefing note for the mayor: the office now supports the extension of the weekend bus service to the harbour district, reversing the advice given in April. The note adds that a revised revenue estimate, received last week, is the reason for the change.

questions.stem: Which assessment of this briefing note is most accurate?

options.text: The note is incomplete because it does not reproduce the April advice in full.
options.misconception: demands verbatim reproduction where a reference would do

options.text: The note records the change, the earlier position, and the reason, which is what the record requires.
The note is adequate because it reports the current position to the mayor clearly.
options.misconception: treats a current-position brief as a change record

options.text: The note is misleading because it uses the phrase now supports for a decision taken earlier.
options.misconception: invents a hidden decision with no support in the text

questions.explanation: The note names the present position, points back to the earlier advice and gives the reason. Reproducing the April text in full is unnecessary when it is clearly identified.
questions.hint: Check for the new position, the old one, and the reason.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Naming a change and recording it
questions.learningObjective: Detect a change that a draft describes without naming
questions.stem: In a planner's draft, the office's view has been informed by recent engagement without saying what the office thought before or thinks now. Which revision would name the change properly?

options.text: The office no longer recommends the twelve-minute cycle, having earlier supported it.
Recent engagement has informed the office's view, which now reflects the current evidence base.
options.misconception: keeps the vagueness while sounding more confident

options.text: The office's view continues to be shaped by modelling, engagement, and community feedback together.
options.misconception: lists influences as though naming them were naming a change

options.text: The twelve-minute cycle remains the recommendation, adjusted after recent engagement.
options.misconception: smuggles in a revision while denying that anything changed

questions.explanation: A change is named when the record states the earlier position, the later one and the ground of the move. The other versions preserve the vagueness or deny that anything changed.
questions.hint: State the earlier view, the later view, and the basis.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A synthesis that leaves the writer's position revised
questions.learningObjective: Write a concluding sentence that records a revised position
questions.stem: A planner must close a synthesis that began from a firm view that the Mill Lane scheme would fail. Which concluding sentence best records the revised position?

options.text: The Mill Lane scheme will fail, as this office argued at the outset of the consultation.
options.misconception: reasserts the starting view as though nothing had moved it

options.text: The scheme's viability depends on the freight traffic figures, which the two studies measure differently.
options.misconception: leaves the reader with a question and no position at all

options.text: We now judge the scheme viable if the freight diversion is maintained, reversing our earlier view.
The two studies are valuable contributions to the debate about traffic on the Mill Lane corridor.
options.misconception: praises the sources without stating the writer's conclusion

questions.explanation: A concluding sentence that records the revision names the earlier view, the later one and the condition attached to it. Reasserting the start leaves the writer's position unstated.
questions.hint: Name the old view, the new one, and the condition.
